Oxygen. A highly reactive, electronegative nonmetal that is the third most abundant element in the universe by mass and the most abundant element in Earth's crust, oceans, and biosphere. It forms a colorless, odorless diatomic gas essential for aerobic respiration in most living organisms. Its high reactivity means it forms oxides with nearly every other element, driving both combustion and corrosion. It also exists as ozone, a triatomic form that creates a protective layer in the stratosphere absorbing harmful ultraviolet radiation.

Carl Wilhelm Scheele discovered oxygen in seventeen seventy-two, calling it "fire air," and Joseph Priestley independently discovered it in seventeen seventy-four. Priestley published first after isolating it by heating mercuric oxide. In seventeen seventy-seven, Antoine Lavoisier named the element and correctly identified it as a chemical element, disproving the phlogiston theory of combustion once and for all. On the Pauling scale of electronegativity, oxygen scores three point four four, second only to fluorine, making it an exceptionally powerful oxidizing agent. In liquid and solid states, oxygen displays paramagnetism—this is the property that allows liquid oxygen to be attracted to and suspended between the poles of a strong magnet. Besides the familiar diatomic form, oxygen exists as ozone, which forms in the stratosphere when sunlight splits diatomic oxygen, and this ozone layer absorbs UV-B radiation. Via photosynthesis, water molecules are split by light-dependent reactions in cyanobacteria, algae, and plants, releasing oxygen gas. Around two point four billion years ago, the Great Oxidation Event dramatically altered Earth's atmospheric composition as oxygen accumulated, causing a mass extinction of anaerobic organisms. In aerobic respiration, oxygen serves as the terminal electron acceptor in the electron transport chain, being reduced to form water. Carbon and oxygen form carbon dioxide, which plants convert to glucose through photosynthesis, releasing oxygen. Hydrogen combines with oxygen to form water, the universal solvent of life. Iron reacts with oxygen and water to form rust—hydrated iron oxide. Oxygen was discovered when Joseph Priestley heated mercuric oxide. Helium undergoes fusion in massive stars through helium-burning processes to create oxygen. Ozone is the triatomic allotrope of oxygen that blocks ultraviolet light.
